nameStory: The six-spotted orbweaver gets its name from the six distinctive pale spots arranged in two neat rows across its bright green abdomen. These spots look almost like tiny polka dots painted on its emerald body, making this spider one of the most recognizable orbweavers in New England. The pattern is so consistent that once you've seen those six spots, you'll never forget this charming little web-spinner.
description: The six-spotted orbweaver is a small, bright green spider that builds classic circular webs between plants and shrubs. Adults are typically about the size of a pea, with females being slightly larger than males. Their most striking feature is their vibrant green coloration with six pale yellowish or white spots arranged in two rows down the back of their round abdomen. These spiders belong to the cucumber spider group, named for their fresh green color that resembles a cucumber's skin.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Six pale yellowish-white spots arranged in two neat rows down the bright green abdomen - this pattern is unmistakable and remains consistent across individuals

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Round, plump abdomen that feels firm to the touch when gently observed, with a bright emerald green color that looks almost artificial in sunlight

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Classic circular orb web, usually small and delicate, often built horizontally or at a slight angle between plant stems about 1-3 feet off the ground

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider, roughly pea-sized, with females reaching about 6-7mm and males slightly smaller at 4-5mm in body length

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in center of web during daylight hours, remaining quite still until prey is caught, then moves with quick, precise movements

habitat: Look for six-spotted orbweavers in gardens, forest edges, meadows, and shrublands throughout New England. They prefer areas with dense vegetation where they can string their webs between plant stems, particularly favoring spots with good morning sunlight. You'll often find them in berry patches, ornamental gardens, and along woodland borders where there's a mix of grasses, herbs, and low shrubs.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring as temperatures warm, starting to build their first webs of the season among emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible in their webs. This is the best time to spot their distinctive six-spotted pattern as they sit prominently in their orb webs.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs in early fall, with females producing egg sacs. Adults begin to disappear as cold weather approaches, with most dying after the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Eggs overwinter in protected locations. No adult spiders are active, as they cannot survive freezing temperatures.

funFact: Six-spotted orbweavers are found on four different continents - North America, Europe, Asia, and parts of Russia - making them one of the most widely distributed orb weaver species in the world, yet they maintain their exact same six-spot pattern everywhere they're found.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small green spiders, but the six pale spots in two rows make this species unmistakable once you know what to look for. Remember the rhyme: 'Six spots in rows, that's how this green spider goes.' No other common New England spider has this exact spot pattern on a bright green body.
contextualKnowledge: This spider belongs to the cucumber spider group (genus Araniella), all named for their fresh green coloration that resembles cucumber skin. Despite the name 'six-spotted,' some individuals may have spots that are very faint or occasionally merged, but the two-row pattern on the green abdomen remains diagnostic.
compareHints: As the only member of the cucumber spider genus commonly found in New England, the six-spotted orbweaver is most easily confused with other small green orbweavers. However, other green orbweavers lack the distinctive six-spot pattern and tend to be either unmarked or have different marking patterns like stripes or irregular blotches rather than the neat, symmetrical spots of this species.
